tagline: A river road links Washington’s estate, tidal wetlands and presidential memorials.
intro: The George Washington Memorial Parkway follows the Potomac from Mount Vernon toward McLean, with Washington Street carrying the route through Alexandria. Its riverbank stretches include overlooks toward Georgetown and the Potomac Palisades. The National Park Service describes a road designed for recreational driving that connects historic sites and wildlife habitat. For this 25-mile All-American Road, the Federal Highway Administration allows an hour without stops or a full day visiting places along the way.

Alexandria advocates formed the Mount Vernon Avenue Association in 1887 to promote a national road to Washington’s estate. The later Bureau of Public Roads campaign gained momentum as Washington’s 1932 bicentennial approached. Consultants Gilmore David Clarke and Jay Downer proposed a winding road with plantings, historic pullouts and scenic overlooks. The first segment opened informally that January, with President Herbert Hoover leading twelve cars to Mount Vernon. Northern sections followed mainly in the 1950s and 1960s.

Start at Mount Vernon’s traffic circle and travel north past Fort Hunt and Dyke Marsh toward Jones Point and Alexandria. Much of the southern route uses the former Washington, Alexandria and Mount Vernon Railway right-of-way. Beyond Washington Street, the parkway returns to the river, passes the airport and Roosevelt Island, and continues to the Capital Beltway.

moments.title: Dyke Marsh
moments.text: Dyke Marsh takes its name from nineteenth-century earthen perimeter walls built to keep tides off land used for crops and livestock. Dredging in the 1950s and 1960s changed its size and shape again. The surviving freshwater wetland lies between Mount Vernon and Old Town Alexandria, under National Park Service management. Non-native vines, including porcelain berry and Japanese honeysuckle, have begun smothering parts of the floodplain forest. Haul Road leads into the marsh, where shoreline erosion is visible along the trail. Narrow-leafed cattails dominate the vegetation; red-winged blackbirds nest among them.

moments.title: Jones Point Light
moments.text: Jones Point Light is a one-story house with a lantern on its roof, built in 1855 to warn naval ships approaching the Washington Navy Yard. In 1926, a nearby steel skeletal tower replaced its working light. That replacement beacon worked for ten years before it, too, was discontinued. An older marker beside it records a different use of the riverbank. The District of Columbia’s 1791–1792 boundary survey began at Jones Point, and its south cornerstone remains in the seawall next to the lighthouse. Both lighthouse and cornerstone entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1980.

moments.title: Theodore Roosevelt Island
moments.text: The woodland on Theodore Roosevelt Island was deliberately planned. In the 1930s, landscape architects turned overgrown farmland into a forest memorial to the president. Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. developed the landscape plan, and the Civilian Conservation Corps cleared much of the island by 1935. The formal memorial, dedicated in 1967, includes Paul Manship’s seventeen-foot Roosevelt statue. Four large stone monoliths carry Roosevelt quotations, and two fountains form part of the memorial’s design. A footbridge from Arlington leads to trails through wooded uplands and swampy bottomlands, with a boardwalk through wet ground.
